Start from the reference class, not the story. The class here is small industrial suppliers reporting one strong quarter and guiding higher into the next. In that class, a single quarter of 12.5 percent revenue growth reverts more often than it compounds; supplier order books are lumpy, and a customer pulling orders forward looks identical to structural demand in one quarter of data.

The record gives exactly one year-on-year observation: 900000000 against 800000000 of revenue, 120000000 against 95000000 of net income. That is a sample of one. The outlook of 950000000 is management's own number, and outlooks in this class skew optimistic precisely when a valuation debate is running.

What would move this subject out of the base case: a second and third quarter of the same growth, or independent evidence of demand (the record carries none - capital spending and short interest are both declared gaps). Until then, the 100.00 price near the 104.00 high assumes the rare outcome. The base case for one-quarter accelerations at twelve times annualized earnings is a flattish price with a wide range, not a compounding one.
